AWS: Amazon ECR ​

Verified against primary documentation on 2026-10-16.

Repository names ​

A private repository name "may be specified on its own (such as nginx-web-app) or it can be prepended with a namespace" such as project-a/nginx-web-app. The API enforces a length of 2 to 256 characters and this pattern (CreateRepository):

txt
[a-z0-9]+((\.|_|__|-+)[a-z0-9]+)*(\/[a-z0-9]+((\.|_|__|-+)[a-z0-9]+)*)*

So each /-separated segment is lowercase letters and digits joined by single ., _, __ or runs of -, and it cannot start or end with a separator. Nesting with / has no stated depth limit beyond the total length, and "using a double forward slash isn't supported" (Creating a private repository). The same page says the name "must start with a letter", but the API pattern accepts a leading digit. The two disagree and this file does not settle which one the service enforces.

The registry host is <aws_account_id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com, and a push reference is that host followed by the repository name and tag, as in docker push aws_account_id.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/prefix/my-new-repository:tag (same page). The repository name is the whole path after the host, so images/shop/api and wasm-components/acme/greeter are both valid names.

A Helm chart is pushed with helm push <chart>.tgz oci://<host>/, and the repository must already exist with "the name you used when creating the Helm chart" (Pushing a Helm chart). The documented example pushes to the bare host and so names the repository after the chart alone. Pushing to oci://<host>/charts/<namespace> and letting Helm append the chart name gives the repository charts/<namespace>/<name>. The ECR page does not show that form, so it rests on Helm's behavior, not on AWS documentation.

Creating repositories ​

Without a matching template, a push to a repository that does not exist fails: "When there isn't a repository creation template that matches the target repository for an image push, Amazon ECR will not create a repository with default settings" (Repository creation templates). With a template, a push "will automatically create the repository for you using the predefined settings of your repository creation template".

A template has an appliedFor list of PULL_THROUGH_CACHE, CREATE_ON_PUSH and REPLICATION, and a prefix. Matching works on the namespace:

  • A prefix of prod/team applies to repositories beginning with prod/team/. "There is always an assumed / applied to the end of the prefix."
  • When two templates match, the longer one wins: with prod and prod/team, the prod/team template applies to names starting with prod/team/.
  • ROOT as the prefix applies "to all repositories in your registry that don't have an associated creation template".
  • A template prefix may be up to 256 characters (CreateRepositoryCreationTemplate).

A template carries tag mutability and its exclusion filters, encryption, a repository policy, a lifecycle policy (up to 30720 characters) and resource tags. Its settings "are only applied during repository creation and don't have any effect on existing repositories". Using resource tags or KMS in a template also needs a repository creation role.

Pull through cache rules ​

A rule maps an ECR repository prefix to an upstream registry. Supported upstreams are Amazon ECR Public, the Kubernetes registry and Quay without authentication, Docker Hub, Azure Container Registry, GitHub Container Registry, GitLab Container Registry and Chainguard with a Secrets Manager secret, and Amazon ECR with an IAM role (Pull through cache). The API names them ecr, ecr-public, quay, k8s, docker-hub, github-container-registry, azure-container-registry, gitlab-container-registry and chainguard (CreatePullThroughCacheRule).

  • The ecrRepositoryPrefix takes the same grammar as a repository name, so it may contain /, but its length is 2 to 30 characters, not 256. A prefix such as mirrors/docker-hub fits.
  • A rule yields repositories named <prefix>/<upstream-repository-name>, for example docker-hub/<upstream-repository-name>. The API notes "there is always an assumed /" at the end of the prefix.
  • For Docker Hub official images "the /library prefix must be included", so the pull is <host>/docker-hub/library/<image>:<tag> (Pulling with a pull through cache).
  • Rules are created per Region. A prefix can be a multi-segment path in the API pattern. The documentation's examples use single-segment prefixes only, so a multi-segment prefix such as mirrors/docker-hub is allowed by the pattern and not shown in a worked example.
  • The repository is created on first pull. Its settings come from a template whose prefix matches, and the page says to use "the repository prefix you specify during rule creation" as the template prefix. With no template the defaults apply: tag immutability off, AES-256, no repository or lifecycle policy.

Refresh from upstream follows the tag: "For subsequent pull requests of the cached image with a given tag, Amazon ECR checks the upstream registry for a new version of the image with that specific tag and attempts to update the image in your private registry at least once every 24 hours." A pull inside the 24-hour window is served from the cache without contacting the upstream, and if the update fails "the last cached image will still be pulled". Template and rule pages recommend MUTABLE for these repositories, since "turning on image tag immutability for repositories using a pull through cache rule will prevent Amazon ECR from updating images using the same tag". Pushing directly into a cache repository "is not a supported pattern".

Tag immutability ​

The repository-level setting accepts MUTABLE, IMMUTABLE, IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION and MUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION (PutImageTagMutability). With immutability on, a push of an existing tag returns ImageTagAlreadyExistsException (Image tag mutability).

The console describes the exclusion fields this way. With Immutable chosen, the exclusion box lets you "enable tag updates for a few immutable tags", and with Mutable chosen it lets you "disable tag updates for a few mutable tags". Both take tag names "or use wildcards (*) to match multiple similar tags". The API form of the first case is IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION plus imageTagMutabilityExclusionFilters, and the page's own CLI example is:

sh
aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --repository-name name \
  --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION \
  --image-tag-mutability-exclusion-filters filterType=WILDCARD,filter=latest

Filter facts (ImageTagMutabilityExclusionFilter):

  • filterType has the single value WILDCARD.
  • filter is 1 to 128 characters matching ^[0-9a-zA-Z._*-]{1,128}$. Letters, digits, ., _, - and * are allowed, which covers latest, canary and *.x.
  • A repository, template or update call takes at most 5 filters.
  • Filters apply to the whole repository. The documentation says individual tag settings "aren't supported", so exemption is by filter only.

Repository creation templates take the same imageTagMutability and filter fields, so a create-on-push template can create repositories already immutable with the exemptions in place.

The documentation does not say whether * matches across . or how many wildcards a filter may hold, so *.x matching 1.x is the natural reading and not a stated example. A filter such as *.x would also match 1.4.x. It does not match 1.4.0. Variant tags such as latest-debug are not covered by latest and need a filter of their own, and a broad filter such as *-debug would also exempt 1.4.0-debug. These two points are inferences from the filter syntax.

Lifecycle policies ​

A policy is a JSON list of rules, each with a unique rulePriority, a selection and an action (Lifecycle policy properties).

  • tagStatus is tagged, untagged or any. tagged requires a tagPrefixList or a tagPatternList.
  • tagPatternList takes strings that "may contain wildcards (*)", with "a maximum limit of four wildcards (*) per string". The page calls it "best practice" for tagged images. prod* matches prod, prod1 and production-team1.
  • tagPrefixList takes plain prefixes, so prod matches prod, prod1 and so on. It is only valid when no tagPatternList is given, and a rule uses either list, "but not both" (How lifecycle policies work).
  • With several tags in one list, "only the images with all specified tags are selected".
  • countType: sinceImagePushed with countUnit: days and a positive countNumber expires images older than that many days. 0 is not accepted. The action is {"type": "expire"}.
  • Rules are all evaluated, then applied by priority, lowest number first. "An image that matches the tagging requirements of a rule cannot be expired or archived by a rule with a lower priority." A rule with tagStatus: any must have the highest rulePriority value, so it runs last.
  • Expiry happens "within 24 hours after they meet the expiration criteria", so a policy is not exact to the hour.

Expiring pr- builds after N days, taken from the documented syntax (Examples, whose age example expires prod* images after 14 days):

json
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Expire pull request builds",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "tagged",
        "tagPatternList": ["pr-*"],
        "countType": "sinceImagePushed",
        "countUnit": "days",
        "countNumber": 14
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    }
  ]
}

The rule lists one pattern because "only the images with all specified tags are selected", so ["pr-*", "0.0.0-pr-*"] would select only images carrying both tags. Charts live in their own repository and take the same rule with 0.0.0-pr-* instead. The documentation's example with ["alpha*", "beta*"] shows the all-patterns behavior.

Keeping release images is by exclusion from the match, not by a "keep" action. A rule selects only images whose tag matches its list, so a rule on pr-* cannot select an image tagged only 1.4.0 or only <commit>. To make the guarantee explicit, a higher-priority rule can select the release pattern with an imageCountMoreThan count above any realistic value, since an image matched by a higher-priority rule cannot be expired by a lower one. The documentation states the priority rule but gives no example of this protect-by-priority use, so that construction is an inference.

Referrers follow their subject: "When reference artifacts are present in a repository, Amazon ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire or archive those artifacts within 24 hours of the deletion or archival of the subject image." Lifecycle policy can also be set in a repository creation template, so created repositories start with the pr- rule in place.

Signatures and referrers ​

ECR supports OCI Image and Distribution specification 1.1, including reference types, in all commercial and GovCloud Regions and in ECR Public (announcement, 27 June 2024). Reference artifacts "can be pulled the same way images are pulled", and per the AWS Open Source blog they live in the same repository as the subject, appear in aws ecr describe-images, and are replicated with it on push (Diving into OCI image and distribution 1.1 support). The ListImageReferrers API lists the artifacts for a subject digest, and its documented example response is a Sigstore bundle, with artifactTypeapplication/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json and a predicate type of https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1 (ListImageReferrers). That is AWS documentation showing a cosign-produced artifact stored as a referrer of an ECR image.

Related facts:

  • AWS's own signing path is AWS Signer, either managed signing on push or manual signing with the Notation CLI. Both "store both your container images and the signatures in your private repositories" (Sign images).
  • "Each signature counts as 1 artifact against the images per repository quota."
  • Pull through cache repositories carry the upstream's referrers. The cache returns them through ListImageReferrers and rechecks them upstream at least every 6 hours, a shorter window than the 24 hours for the image itself.
  • Replication copies referrers with the image. This ADR's rule to copy signatures when an artifact moves to another registry still applies to registries outside ECR replication.

Not verified ​

  • A statement in the AWS documentation that names cosign and says it works against ECR. The evidence is the Sigstore bundle in the ListImageReferrers example. How cosign chooses between the referrers API and the legacy .sig tag depends on the cosign version and its flags, and that is cosign documentation, not AWS documentation.
  • Whether the /library and multi-segment prefix behavior holds for a pull through cache prefix of mirrors/docker-hub. The API pattern allows it, and no AWS page shows it.
  • The exact wildcard semantics of an exclusion filter beyond the allowed character set and the 5-filter limit.
  • Whether a charts namespace works with helm push oci://<host>/charts. AWS documents only the bare-host form.
  • Whether a repository name may start with a digit, given the prose and pattern disagree.
